A prerogative is a special right or power that belongs exclusively to a particular person, group, or institution — usually because of who they are, what position they hold, or what role they play. It's a right that others cannot take away, override, or question.

The single most important word to attach to "prerogative" is: exclusive. It's not just a right — it's a right that is yours alone in a given situation.

Think of it this way. Many people have the right to vote. That's just called a right. But a judge has the power to decide what sentence a criminal receives — no one else in the courtroom can do that. That is a prerogative. It belongs to the judge because of the role they hold.

So a prerogative is a right that comes with a specific position, rank, or authority, and that right is yours to exercise without needing anyone else's permission or approval.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Formal / Official Prerogative

This is when a prerogative belongs to someone because of an official role or position of power.

  • A president may have the prerogative to pardon criminals — no court can stop it.
  • A CEO has the prerogative to make the final call on major company decisions.
  • A doctor has the prerogative to determine the right treatment for a patient.

In each case, the person exercises this right by virtue of their position. It comes with the job. Others may disagree, but they generally cannot override it.

2. Personal / Informal Prerogative

This is a slightly softer but very common use of the word. Here, a prerogative simply means a personal right to make a choice — especially one that others may question, but that you are fully entitled to make.

  • "She decided not to explain her reasons. That's her prerogative."
  • "I changed my mind about going. It's my prerogative."

Here, the word is basically saying: "This is my choice to make, and it's not anyone else's place to challenge it." It asserts personal authority over your own decisions.
The Key Flavour of the Word

What makes "prerogative" richer than just saying "right" is the feeling it carries. When you call something a prerogative, you're communicating two things at once:

  1. This right is mine exclusively — not shared by just anyone.
  2. This right is not up for debate — it is understood, accepted, and respected.

This gives the word a slight tone of authority, dignity, and finality. When someone invokes their prerogative, the conversation about whether they can do something is essentially over. The only question left is what they will decide.

You'll very often hear: "It is someone's prerogative to..."

This phrasing introduces the prerogative and signals that the person is fully within their rights to do what follows.

  • "It is the committee's prerogative to reject any application without giving a reason."
  • "It's your prerogative to leave the job if you feel it's right for you."
How to Tell You've Understood It Correctly

Ask yourself this test question when you encounter the word: "Is this a right or power that belongs specifically to this person or group, and that others are not really in a position to deny or override?"

If yes — that's a prerogative.

A prerogative is an exclusive right or power that belongs to a specific person or group. It often comes with a position of authority, but it can also simply mean a personal right to make your own choices. The heart of the word is exclusivity and unquestionability — it's yours, others recognize it as yours, and invoking it settles the matter of whether you're allowed to do something.
